'''Jean-Pierre Demailly''' (25 September 1957 – 17 March 2022) was a French [[mathematician]] who worked in [[complex geometry]]. He was a professor at [[Université Grenoble Alpes]] and a permanent member of the [[French Academy of Sciences]].

==Early life and education==
Demailly was born on 25 September 1957 in [[Péronne, Somme|Péronne]], France.<ref name="CV">{{cite web |url=http://www-fourier.ujf-grenoble.fr/~demailly/CV.html |title=Curriculum Vitae |website=Jean-Pierre Demailly |lang=fr |accessdate=19 March 2022}}</ref><ref name="academy-profile"/> He attended the Lycée de Péronne from 1966 to 1973 and the [[Lycée Faidherbe]] from 1973 to 1975.<ref name="CV"/> He entered the [[École Normale Supérieure]] in 1975, where he received his [[agrégation]] in 1977 and graduated in 1979.<ref name="academy-profile">{{cite web |url=https://www.academie-sciences.fr/pdf/membre/DemaillyJP_bio.pdf |title=Jean-Pierre Demailly |website=[[French Academy of Sciences]] |lang=fr |accessdate=19 March 2022}}</ref> During this time, he received an undergraduate ''[[Licence (France)|licence]]'' degree from [[Paris Diderot University]] in 1976 and a ''[[diplôme d'études approfondies]]'' under [[Henri Skoda]] at the [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]] in 1979.<ref name="CV"/> He received his ''[[Doctorat d'État]]'' in 1982 under the direction of Skoda at the Pierre and Marie Curie University, with thesis "Sur différents aspects de la positivité en analyse complexe".<ref name="academy-profile"/><ref>{{MathGenealogy|64092}}</ref>

==Career==
Demailly became a professor at [[Université Grenoble Alpes]] in 1983.<ref name="academy-profile"/> He served as the editor-in-chief of the ''[[Annales de l'Institut Fourier]]'' from 1998 to 2006 and the editor-in-chief of ''[[Comptes Rendus Mathématique]]'' from 2010 to 2015.<ref name="academy-profile"/><ref name="notices"/> He was also an editor for ''[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]'' from 1997 to 2002.<ref name="academy-profile"/>

He was the director of the Institut Fourier from 2003 to 2006.<ref name="academy-profile"/> From June 2003 onwards, he led the ''Groupe de réflexion interdisciplinaire sur les programmes'' (GRIP), which ran experimental classes in primary schools.<ref name="academy-profile"/>

==Research==
Demailly's mathematical works primarily concerned [[complex analytic geometry]], using techniques from [[complex geometry]] with applications to [[algebraic geometry]] and [[number theory]].<ref name="academy-profile"/> He also wrote and co-authored several [[Unix]] and [[Linux]] programs and libraries starting in the 1990s, including ''[[XPaint]]'', ''sunclock'', and ''[[dmg2img]]''.<ref name="academy-profile"/>

===Kählerian geometry===
One main topic of Demailly's research is [[Pierre Lelong]]'s generalization of the notion of a [[Kähler form]] to allow forms with singularities, known as [[current (mathematics)|current]]s. In particular, for a [[compact space|compact]] [[complex manifold]] <math>X</math>, an element of the [[Dolbeault cohomology]] group <math>H^{1,1}(X,\R)</math> is called pseudo-effective if it is represented by a closed positive (1,1)-[[current (mathematics)|current]] (where "positive" means "nonnegative" in this phrase), or [[Ample line bundle#Big line bundles|big]] if it is represented by a strictly positive (1,1)-current; these definitions generalize the corresponding notions for holomorphic [[invertible sheaf|line bundles]] on [[projective varieties]]. Demailly's regularization theorem says, in particular, that any big class can be represented by a Kähler current with analytic singularities.<ref>Demailly (1992); Demailly (2012), Corollary 14.13.</ref>

Such analytic results have had many applications to [[algebraic geometry]]. In particular, Boucksom, Demailly, Păun, and Peternell showed that a [[smooth scheme|smooth]] complex projective variety <math>X</math> is [[uniruled variety|uniruled]] if and only if its [[canonical bundle]] <math>K_X</math> is not pseudo-effective.<ref>Boucksom et al. (2013); Lazarsfeld (2004), Corollary 11.4.20.</ref>

===Multiplier ideals===
For a singular metric on a line bundle, Nadel, Demailly, and [[Yum-Tong Siu]] developed the concept of the [[multiplier ideal]], which describes where the metric is most singular. There is an analog of the [[Kodaira vanishing theorem]] for such a metric, on compact or noncompact complex manifolds.<ref>Lazarsfeld (2004), Ch. 9; Demailly (2012), Theorem 5.11.</ref> This led to the first effective criteria for a line bundle on a complex projective variety <math>X</math> of any dimension <math>n</math> to be [[very ample]], that is, to have enough global sections to give an embedding of <math>X</math> into [[complex projective space|projective space]]. For example, Demailly showed in 1993 that <math>2K_X+ 12n^nL</math> is very ample for any [[ample line bundle]] ''L'', where addition denotes the [[tensor product]] of line bundles. The method has inspired later improvements in the direction of the [[Fujita conjecture]].<ref>Demailly (2012), Theorem 7.4.</ref>

===Kobayashi hyperbolicity===
Demailly used the technique of [[jet (mathematics)|jet]] differentials introduced by Green and [[Phillip Griffiths]] to prove [[Kobayashi metric|Kobayashi hyperbolicity]] for various projective varieties. For example, Demailly and El Goul showed that a very general complex surface <math>X</math> of [[degree of an algebraic variety|degree]] at least 21 in projective space <math>\mathbb{CP}^3</math> is hyperbolic; equivalently, every [[holomorphic map]] <math>\Complex \to X</math> is constant.<ref>Demailly & El Goul (2000).</ref> For any variety <math>X</math> of [[general type]], Demailly showed that every holomorphic map <math>\Complex \to X</math> satisfies some (in fact, many) [[algebraic differential equation]]s.<ref>Demailly (2011); Demailly (2012), Theorem 9.5.</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Demailly received the [[CNRS Bronze Medal]] in 1981,<ref name="academy-profile"/> the {{ill|Prix Mergier-Bourdeix|fr}} from the [[French Academy of Sciences]] in 1994,<ref name="academy-profile"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.academie-sciences.fr/archivage_site/activite/prix/laureat_mergier.pdf |title=Prix Mergier Bourdeix |website=[[French Academy of Sciences]] |accessdate=19 March 2022}}</ref> the [[Humboldt Prize]] in 1996,<ref name="academy-profile"/> the [[Simion Stoilow Prize]] from the [[Romanian Academy of Sciences]] in 2006,<ref name="academy-profile"/> the [[Stefan Bergman Prize]] from the [[American Mathematical Society]] in 2015,<ref name="academy-profile"/><ref name="notices">{{cite journal |title=Mathematics People |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=63 |issue=4 |year=2016 |pages=445–447}}</ref> and the [[Heinz Hopf Prize]] from [[ETH]] in 2021.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://math.ethz.ch/news-and-events/events/lecture-series/heinz-hopf-prize-and-lectures.html |title=Heinz Hopf Prize and Lectures |website=[[ETH Zurich]] |accessdate=19 March 2022}}</ref>

Demailly was elected a correspondent of the [[French Academy of Sciences]] in 1994 and then became a permanent member in 2007.<ref name="academy-profile"/><ref name="academie-sciences">{{cite web|url=http://www.academie-sciences.fr/fr/Liste-des-membres-de-l-Academie-des-sciences-/-D/jean-pierre-demailly.html|publisher=academie-sciences.fr|title=Jean-Pierre Demailly &#124; Liste des membres de l'Académie des sciences / D &#124; Listes par ordre alphabétique &#124; Listes des membres &#124; Membres &#124; Nous connaître|accessdate=2 March 2017}}</ref> He was an invited speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1994 and a plenary speaker in 2006.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.mathunion.org/icm-plenary-and-invited-speakers |title=ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers |website=[[International Mathematical Union]] |accessdate=19 March 2021}}</ref>

In 2024, the [[Jean-Pierre Demailly prize for open science in mathematics]] is created in his honor. It is awarded every two years.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Badolato |first=Anne-Marie |date=2024-05-29 |title=Prix science ouverte en mathématiques |url=https://www.ouvrirlascience.fr/prix-jean-pierre-demailly-pour-la-science-ouverte-en-mathematiques |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=Ouvrir la Science |language=fr}}</ref>

In 2025, the [[Société mathématique de France]] published a special issue of its gazette in his memory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jean-Pierre Demailly {{!}} Société Mathématique de France |url=https://smf.emath.fr/publications/jean-pierre-demailly |access-date=2025-05-21 |website=smf.emath.fr}}</ref>

==Death==
Demailly died on 17 March 2022.<ref name="smf-death">{{cite web |url=https://smf.emath.fr/actualites-smf/deces-de-jean-pierre-demailly |title=Décès de Jean-Pierre Demailly |website=[[Société mathématique de France]] |lang=fr |date=18 March 2022 |accessdate=19 March 2022}}</ref>
